prompt: Write a reflective essay of about 300 words on your experience in a group project this semester, covering teamwork, conflict and what you would do differently.
text:
Looking back on the group project for Intro to Marketing, I think the biggest thing I learned is that not everyone works the same way. At the start we split the work into four parts but nobody really checked in with each other until like two days before it was due. Me and Priya ended up doing most of the slides at the last minute which was stressful.

The part I was responsible for was the market research section. I found most of the data myself from the census site and some industry reports from the library database. I think my section was ok but it could have been better if I had started earlier. I didnt really ask anyone for help with the survey questions and I should have.

Looking at the group now, I think we did well in the presentation. Our professor said our recommendations were clear and the visuals were good. But the process was pretty messy. Tomas kept saying he would send his part and then he didnt until the night before. That made me kind of annoyed at first but then I realized I hadnt been great at communicating either.

If I did it again I would set up a shared calendar on day one and have short check ins every week. Also I would make sure we agree on who does what before we start instead of just saying yeah sure. I think group work is hard but it is useful because in real jobs you also have to work with people who dont do things the way you want.

prompt: Write a reflective essay of about 300 words on your experience in a group project this semester, covering teamwork, conflict and what you would do differently.
text:
In this reflective essay I want to explain about my experience in the group project for the marketing course. At the beginning, we were four people in the group and we did not know each other very well. Our teacher gave us the topic of a new coffee brand, and everybody was excited. However, the problem was that nobody wanted to be the leader.

I was the person who wrote the first draft of the plan. My friend Elif did the research part because she is very good at finding informations from the internet. Ahmet was responsible for the presentation, but he is always late for meetings, so we had some problems. I think it was difficult for me to tell him directly that he must come on time. In Turkish culture we often avoid to say negative things to friends, so I did not say anything for two weeks.

When I think about this now, I learned that communication is very important in a group. I am agree that the project was successful at the end, but we could have made it easier if we talked earlier. Also, I learned how to divide the tasks. In the beginning we made the mistake to give everything to one person, and she became very tired.

My opinion is that next time I will make a clear plan on the first day. I will write the deadlines in the group chat and ask everyone to confirm. I think this will help us to avoid stress. Group work is not only about the final result, but also about how we work with the people around us.

prompt: Write a reflective essay of about 300 words on your experience in a group project this semester, covering teamwork, conflict and what you would do differently.
text:
Looking back on our group project for Organizational Behavior, I'm struck by how much the process taught me about teamwork than the final grade did. We were a team of four, and at the start we split the work evenly on paper, but in practice the workload was anything but even. Within the first week, it was clear that Daniel had taken on the lion's share of the research, while I'd drifted toward the editing role almost by accident.

What worked well was our decision to meet in person every Thursday. Those sessions gave us a chance to talk through disagreements before they became resentments. When Maya and I clashed over whether to use interviews or survey data, we hashed it out over coffee and reached a compromise that neither of us had initially wanted, but that ended up strengthening the final report.

What didn't work was our communication outside of meetings. We relied on a group chat that quickly filled with memes and half-finished thoughts. I'd often wait for a clear answer that never came, and I'd end up making decisions on my own. I don't think anyone was deliberately unhelpful, we just never agreed on how to hold each other accountible.

If I could do it again, I'd definately set clear roles on day one, along with a shared timeline that everyone signed off on. I'd also be more direct about my own limits instead of quietly overcommitting. The project wasn't perfect, but it showed me that good teamwork depends less on talent than on honest, regular communication, and that's a lesson I'll carry into my next job.

prompt: Write a reflective essay of about 300 words on your experience in a group project this semester, covering teamwork, conflict and what you would do differently.
text:
This reflective essay examines my experience as a member of a four-person team during the group project for the course Organizational Behaviour. The project required the team to analyse the leadership structure of a mid-sized manufacturing company and to propose recommendations for improving internal communication. In retrospect, the project provided valuable insight into the dynamics of collaborative work, particularly with respect to role allocation, accountability, and conflict resolution.

At the outset, the team distributed responsibilities according to a provisional plan. However, the allocation proved uneven in practice. Research and analysis were concentrated in the hands of one member, while coordination tasks were not assigned to any individual. Consequently, progress slowed during the middle weeks of the term, and the team was required to revise its timeline. This experience illustrated the importance of establishing explicit responsibilities at an early stage, rather than relying on informal agreements.

Conflict emerged during the selection of the methodology, as two members held opposing views regarding the relative merits of qualitative interviews and quantitative surveys. The disagreement was ultimately resolved through a structured discussion in which each position was evaluated against the research question. Although the outcome was not the preference of any single member, the resulting mixed-methods design strengthened the final report. I now recognise that disagreement, when managed constructively, can improve the quality of collective decision-making.

Reflecting on the project as a whole, I identify two areas for personal development. First, I tend to defer to others when uncertainty arises, which reduced my contribution to strategic decisions. Second, I underestimated the value of regular written updates. Future projects will be approached with a clearer plan for communication, a defined schedule of checkpoints, and a willingness to raise concerns at an earlier stage.

prompt: Summarise a psychology journal article on sleep deprivation and memory, covering aims, method, findings and limitations, in about 250 words.
text:
This article is about how sleep affects memory in college students. The researchers, Hart and Moreno (2019), wanted to see if getting less sleep the night before a test changes how well students remember new words. They had 84 undergraduates learn a list of words and then tested them either the next morning after a full night of sleep or after staying up all night.

The results showed that the students who slept did better on the test, around 15 percent more words recalled on average. The authors say this supports the idea that sleep helps to consolidate memories, which means the brain kind of organizes what you learned while you sleep. They also measured mood and attention, and the sleep deprived group reported feeling more tired but the difference in attention was not very big.

The paper has some limits. The sample was small and all of them were from one university so it might not work for everyone. Also the words were not related to real course material so we dont know if it applies to studying for actual exams. The authors suggest future studies should use more realistic tasks and look at different age groups.

Overall I think the article is useful because it gives evidence for something people say a lot, that pulling an all nighter is bad for studying. But I would like to see a bigger study before I believe it fully.

prompt: Summarise a psychology journal article on sleep deprivation and memory, covering aims, method, findings and limitations, in about 250 words.
text:
Hart and Moreno's 2019 study asks a question most students have probably asked themselves at 3 a.m. before an exam: does pulling an all-nighter actually hurt memory? To find out, the researchers recruited 84 undergraduates, had them memorize a list of words, and then tested them the following morning. Half had slept normally, while the other half stayed awake for the entire night.

The sleep group recalled roughly 15 percent more words than the sleep-deprived group. The authors argue this supports the idea that sleep consolidates memories, essentially giving the brain time to sort and store what was learned. The sleep-deprived participants also reported feeling more fatigued, though differences in attention weren't especially large.

What I found most convincing was the careful design. The comparison was clean, and the outcome measure was simple and direct. That said, the study has obvious limits. It's a small sample from a single university, and the word lists don't resemble actual course material, so it's hard to know how well the findings transfer to real exam preparation. The authors themselves call for more realistic tasks and broader age ranges.

Still, the takeaway seems reasonable: cramming at the expense of sleep is probably a bad trade. I'd want replication before treating the 15 percent figure as settled, but the direction of the effect is plausible and consistant with prior work.

prompt: Summarise a psychology journal article on sleep deprivation and memory, covering aims, method, findings and limitations, in about 250 words.
text:
Hart and Moreno (2019) examine the effect of sleep deprivation on the consolidation of declarative memory in university students. The study addresses a practically significant question, namely whether the loss of a night's sleep following learning impairs subsequent recall of newly acquired information. Eighty-four undergraduate participants studied a list of words and were subsequently assessed the following morning, having either obtained a full night of sleep or remained awake throughout the night.

The authors report that participants in the sleep condition recalled approximately 15 percent more words than those in the sleep-deprived condition. Interpreting these findings within the consolidation framework, the authors propose that sleep facilitates the stabilisation and integration of memory traces after encoding. Self-reported measures indicated greater fatigue among sleep-deprived participants, although the between-group difference in sustained attention was modest and, according to the authors, not statistically robust.

Several methodological limitations temper the conclusions that may be drawn. The sample was relatively small and drawn from a single institution, which constrains generalisability. Moreover, the stimuli consisted of unrelated word lists rather than material resembling academic content, limiting ecological validity with respect to examination preparation. The authors acknowledge these constraints and recommend that subsequent research employ more realistic learning tasks and include a wider range of age groups.

Overall, the article provides a clear and well-structured contribution to the literature on sleep and memory. Its principal value lies in offering experimental evidence for a relationship that is often assumed in applied contexts, although replication with larger and more ecologically valid samples would be required before the effect size is interpreted with confidence.

Table 1 and Figure 2 summarise the reaction rates measured across five temperatures, ranging from 20 to 60 °C. Rates increased steadily from 20 °C up to a peak at 40 °C, where the mean activity reached 0.85 absorbance units per minute. prompt: Write the results paragraph of a lab report on the effect of temperature on catalase activity, referring to Table 1 and Figure 2.
text:
The reaction rates obtained across the five temperature conditions are summarised in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 2. Mean enzymatic activity increased monotonically between 20 °C and 40 °C, from 0.21 to 0.85 absorbance units per minute, indicating a positive relationship between temperature and reaction velocity within this range. Activity subsequently declined sharply, and at 60 °C the measured rate was indistinguishable from zero, which is consistent with irreversible thermal denaturation of the catalytic protein.

With the exception of the 50 °C condition, standard deviations across the three replicate trials were low, suggesting good experimental reproducibility. The 50 °C trial that deviated markedly from the others exhibited visible turbidity in the cuvette, a feature consistent with sample contamination. Owing to time constraints, this measurement was not repeated. It has been retained in the dataset and identified explicitly so that its influence on the fitted curve may be assessed in the discussion.

The overall profile conforms to the expected pattern for enzyme kinetics, in which activity increases with temperature until the thermal stability threshold is exceeded. On the basis of these data, the apparent optimum lies near 40 °C. A more precise estimate would require additional measurements at intermediate temperatures between 35 and 45 °C.

prompt: Write a critique of the film Last Train to Harbor City, assessing direction, script, acting and overall value.
text:
The movie Last Train to Harbor City is supposed to be a thriller but honestly I thought it was more of a slow drama with some action in the middle. The director does a lot with the setting. The train is basically a character itself and the lighting in the tunnel scenes is really good. I liked how they used the sound of the wheels to build tension.

The main problem for me was the script. The main character, Elena, makes a lot of decisions that dont make sense. For example in the second act she just walks into a police station without any reason and then the cops let her go. It felt like the writers needed her to do something so the plot could move forward. The supporting characters were also pretty flat. The conductor is interesting for like five minutes and then he just disappears.

The acting is good though. The actress who plays Elena carries most of the film and you can really see her emotions even when she doesnt say anything. Her scenes with the old man in the dining car were my favorite part.

Overall I would give it maybe a 6 out of 10. Its worth watching for the visuals and the sound design but the story doesnt hold together well. If the writers had cut a few subplots it could have been much tighter.

prompt: Write a critique of the film Last Train to Harbor City, assessing direction, script, acting and overall value.
text:
Last Train to Harbor City markets itself as a taut thriller, but it's really more of a moody character study that happens to take place on a train. That's not necessarily a flaw. Marco Lenz clearly cares about atmosphere, and the film is at its best when it lets the setting do the talking. The tunnel sequences, shot in near darkness with only the headlamps for light, are genuinely unsettling, and the sound design, with the rhythmic clatter of the wheels, builds tension better than most of the film's dialogue does.

The screenplay is another matter. Elena, the protagonist, keeps making choices that don't hold up. In the second act she walks into a police station for no obvious reason, and the officers simply let her go. It's a moment that exists to move the plot forward, not because anything about her character justifies it. The supporting cast suffers too. The conductor is intriguing for about five minutes and then vanishs from the story altogether, which is frustrating given how much the film seems to want him to matter.

What saves the picture is the lead performance. The actress carries nearly every scene, and her face does a lot of work when she has nothing to say. The quiet exchanges with the old man in the dining car are the emotional center of the movie, and they're the moments I found myself thinking about afterward.

I'd give it a six out of ten. It's worth seeing for the craft, but the story needed another draft. Trim two of the subplots and tighten Elena's decision-making, and this could have been a genuinely memorable film.

prompt: Write a critique of the film Last Train to Harbor City, assessing direction, script, acting and overall value.
text:
Last Train to Harbor City is presented as a psychological thriller, though its principal strengths lie in atmosphere and character rather than in suspense. Directed by Marco Lenz, the film uses the confined setting of a night train to produce a sustained sense of isolation, and this is its most successful achievement. The cinematography in the tunnel sequences, which relies on minimal illumination, is particularly effective, and the sound design, in which the rhythmic motion of the wheels is foregrounded, contributes considerably to the film's tension.

The screenplay, however, is less convincing. The protagonist, Elena, repeatedly acts in ways that are difficult to reconcile with her established characterisation. In the second act, for example, she enters a police station without apparent motivation, and her release follows without any plausible explanation. Such moments appear to serve the progression of the plot rather than the logic of the character. Several supporting figures are similarly underdeveloped; the conductor, in particular, receives considerable narrative attention before disappearing from the story without resolution.

The performance of the lead actress is the film's most consistent asset. She sustains the narrative largely through non-verbal expression, and her interactions with the elderly passenger in the dining car offer the most affecting material in the film. These scenes demonstrate a restraint that the remainder of the screenplay does not always match.

In summary, the film succeeds as a work of visual and auditory craft but falls short as a narrative. A more rigorous edit, with fewer subplots and more coherent characterisation, would have considerably strengthened its overall effect. On balance, I would assess it as a competent but uneven contribution to the genre.

prompt: Write a policy memo recommending how the city should cut transport emissions under its climate plan.
text:
Our city has been talking about climate change for years but the actual plans are pretty vague. This memo argues that the council should adopt a stronger policy on reducing emissions from transport, which is the biggest source of local emissions according to the 2023 inventory. The current plan only sets a goal of 20 percent reduction by 2030 without saying how to get there.

There are three options we think are worth considering. The first is expanding the bus network with electric buses. This would cost a lot upfront, about 40 million, but it would cut emissions and also help people who cant afford cars. The second option is a congestion charge in the downtown area, which is what London and Stockholm did and it worked pretty well. The third is building more bike lanes, which is cheap but probably wont make a big difference alone.

Our recommendation is to combine the first two options. The congestion charge can pay for part of the bus expansion, so the net cost to the city is lower. We would also suggest a public consultation before the charge starts because people will be upset about it.

The main risk is that businesses downtown might complain about lower traffic. Some of them might lose customers. But the evidence from other cities suggests that the effects are smaller than people expect, and the air quality improvements are good for everyone.

prompt: Write a policy memo recommending how the city should cut transport emissions under its climate plan.
text:
This memorandum recommends a revised strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the transport sector, which the 2023 municipal emissions inventory identifies as the largest single source of local emissions. The existing climate plan commits the city to a reduction of 20 percent by 2030 but does not specify the instruments through which this target would be achieved. The absence of a defined implementation pathway represents the principal weakness of the current framework.

Three policy options merit consideration. The first is the phased introduction of electric buses across the public transport network. The capital cost is estimated at approximately 40 million, which is significant relative to the municipal budget, but the measure would yield substantial reductions in emissions and improve mobility for residents without private vehicles. The second is a congestion charge applied to the central business district, a model that has produced measurable reductions in traffic volume in London and Stockholm. The third is the expansion of cycling infrastructure, which carries low capital cost but is unlikely to achieve the scale of reduction required in isolation.

It is recommended that the first two options be implemented jointly. Revenue generated by the congestion charge could partially finance the bus programme, thereby reducing the net fiscal burden on the city. Given the likelihood of public resistance, a formal consultation process should precede the introduction of the charge, with clear communication of the expected health and environmental benefits.

The principal risk concerns the commercial sector within the central district, where businesses may anticipate reduced customer volumes. Comparable international experience suggests that such effects tend to be smaller than initially projected. Nevertheless, the council should monitor local economic indicators throughout the first two years of the scheme and be prepared to adjust its design accordingly.

prompt: Analyse a primary source: a 1912 letter from a textile worker during the Lawrence strike. Discuss context, content and reliability.
text:
The source I chose is a letter written by a factory worker in 1912 during the Lawrence textile strike in Massachusetts. The letter was published in a newspaper of the time and it is included in our course reader. The author signs it only with his initials so we dont know his full name, which is a limitation.

The first thing I noticed is the tone. The writer is angry but also very careful, he says things like we are only asking for what is fair and we will keep working if the mill listens. I think he was trying to make the strikers look respectable to the public, which makes sense because newspapers at the time were often hostile to unions. So the letter is probably written with an audience in mind, not just to express his feelings.

The second thing is the content. He lists specific complaints about wages, and mentions the number of hours and the fines for talking on the floor. These details are useful because they give evidence about working conditions that other sources sometimes describe only in general terms.

In terms of reliability I would say the letter is useful but not perfect. It was published by a paper that supported the strikers, so it may be biased. Also one letter cannot represent all workers. Still, it gives a good insight into how workers justified their demands in public.

prompt: Analyse a primary source: a 1912 letter from a textile worker during the Lawrence strike. Discuss context, content and reliability.
text:
The source I've chosen is a letter from a textile worker in Lawrence, Massachusetts, printed in a local newspaper during the 1912 strike. The author signs only with his initials, which is frustrating, since it means we can't verify who he was or what his position in the mill was. Still, the letter is valuable for what it reveals about how strikers presented themselves to the public.

The most striking feature is the tone. The writer is angry, but he's also deliberately measured. He insists that the workers are asking only for fair treatment and that they'll return to their looms if the company listens. That restraint is almost certainly strategic. Newspapers of the period were frequently hostile to organised labour, so a letter like this seems designed to make the strikers look respectable and reasonable rather than radical.

The content is equally useful. He lists low wages, long hours, and fines for talking on the floor, and these specifics give historians concrete evidence about everyday conditions that other sources tend to describe only in general terms. A reference to fines in particular suggests how tightly management controlled workers' behaviour.

As for reliability, I'd say the letter is useful but needs careful handling. The paper that printed it sympathised with the strikers, so the selection may reflect editorial bias. And a single letter from one anonymous worker can't stand in for the experience of thousands. Read alongside union records and company statements, though, it offers a vivid window into the arguments workers made in public.

prompt: Analyse a primary source: a 1912 letter from a textile worker during the Lawrence strike. Discuss context, content and reliability.
text:
This analysis examines a letter written by an anonymous textile worker in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1912, during a major industrial dispute involving the city's mill workforce. The letter was reprinted in a regional newspaper and subsequently included in a published collection of primary sources. The author identifies himself only by initials, a limitation that restricts efforts to establish his occupational position or personal background.

The document is notable first for its tone. Although the writer expresses clear grievances, he adopts a measured and restrained register, emphasising that the strikers seek only equitable treatment and would resume work upon the company's acceptance of reasonable demands. This rhetorical moderation is best understood in the context of contemporary press coverage, which frequently portrayed organised labour as disruptive. The letter may therefore be read as an attempt to frame the strike as a legitimate and respectable campaign addressed to a sceptical public.

The letter's substantive content is equally significant. It enumerates specific grievances concerning wage levels, the length of the working day, and the imposition of fines for conversation on the factory floor. Such details are rare in sources that describe industrial conditions in general terms and provide concrete evidence of the disciplinary regime within the mills.

With respect to reliability, the source must be approached with caution. Its publication in a newspaper sympathetic to the strikers introduces the possibility of editorial selection, and the testimony of a single anonymous worker cannot be taken as representative of the broader workforce. Nonetheless, when read alongside union records and company correspondence, the letter offers valuable insight into the strategies through which workers articulated their claims to a wider audience.

prompt: Answer a marketing case about an organic smoothie chain deciding whether to expand to new cities or grow existing stores.
text:
In this case, the company is a small chain of organic smoothie shops that wants to grow from 4 locations to 10 in two years. The main question is whether they should focus on expanding to new cities or on increasing sales in the existing shops.

My recommendation is to focus on the existing locations first. The reason is that the stores are not at full capacity yet, especially on weekdays between 2 and 5 pm, so there is room to grow without spending a lot on new rent. They also have a loyalty program but only about 15 percent of customers use it. If they improve the app and offer rewards for trying new flavors, they could get more repeat visits.

Second, the company should think about its target market. Right now the brand is marketed to young women, but the case says a lot of their customers are actually men aged 30 to 45 who buy protein smoothies after the gym. I think they should test a campaign aimed at this group using social media ads and partnerships with local gyms.

The risk is that the brand could lose its identity if it tries to appeal to everyone. So I would keep the healthy and natural image but make the messaging more specific for each segment. Expansion can come later once they have the data to show the new stores will work.

prompt: Answer a marketing case about an organic smoothie chain deciding whether to expand to new cities or grow existing stores.
text:
The organisation in this case is a small chain of organic smoothie outlets currently operating four locations and seeking to expand to ten within a two-year period. The central strategic question concerns the allocation of growth investment between geographic expansion and the intensification of performance in existing outlets. It is recommended that the company prioritise the latter.

The rationale rests principally on capacity utilisation. Existing outlets do not operate at full potential, with demand notably weak during weekday afternoons between 14:00 and 17:00. Revenue can therefore be increased without the fixed costs associated with new premises. A further opportunity lies in the loyalty programme, which is currently used by only approximately 15 percent of customers. Enhancing the mobile application and introducing incentives for trialling new products would be expected to raise visit frequency and customer retention.

The analysis also indicates a misalignment between the brand's communications and its actual customer base. Current marketing is directed predominantly at young women, whereas a significant proportion of purchasers are men aged 30 to 45 who consume protein-based smoothies following exercise. A segment-specific campaign employing targeted social media advertising and partnerships with local fitness facilities would address this gap at relatively modest cost, and its effectiveness could be evaluated with precision.

A principal risk is that the brand's identity becomes diluted if it attempts to appeal indiscriminately to all consumers. Accordingly, the company should preserve its established positioning around health and naturalness while adapting messaging to each segment. Expansion to new markets should be deferred until the performance data from existing outlets provides a reliable basis for the investment decision.
